opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For an inference engine, Day-0 support matters because the moment a new open model drops, that's when people are most eager to try it. Developers, researchers, and companies all want to run it right away, benchmark it, and see if it fits their product. If your framework can't serve it on launch day, people go to whatever can, and they often stick with it. So it's a big part of how an open-source project earns trust and adoption.

There's also a technical reason. New models increasingly bring architectural changes: new attention variants, mixture-of-experts layouts, different positional encodings, multimodal components, new quantization formats. Supporting them on Day 0 forces us to keep the engine flexible and well-abstracted, instead of hard-coding assumptions about what a model looks like. That benefits everyone who uses the system later.

And it's really a collaboration story. To have support ready at release, we work with model teams before launch, sometimes for weeks, on correctness, kernels, and performance tuning. That early feedback helps them too. We can catch numerical issues or serving bottlenecks before the public sees the model. When it works well, the model's first impression to the community is fast and correct inference instead of a week of people struggling to get it running. That's good for the model team, for us, and for the whole open ecosystem.

r001.rationale: It says developers, researchers, and companies want to run new models immediately, and that this demand drives adoption and trust in the inference framework.

r002.rationale: It describes immediate user interest and collaboration with model teams, but does not state that this demand propagates through inference providers to Ying Sheng’s team and then onward to model vendors.

fable-5.1.text:
Day-0 compatibility matters because, from the user's perspective, a new model is only useful if they can actually run it the moment it comes out. When a lab releases something like a new Llama or DeepSeek or Qwen model, the first few days are when excitement is highest. People want to download the weights, spin up a server, and start testing. If the serving framework they rely on doesn't support the architecture yet, they either wait or they switch to whatever does support it. So for an inference engine like SGLang, being there on day zero is really about trust. Users need to believe that whatever comes next, they won't be blocked.

There's also a deeper technical reason. New models increasingly ship with architectural changes: new attention variants, different MoE routing, multi-token prediction, new quantization formats. If you only start adapting after release, you discover that your abstractions were built around the previous generation's assumptions. Working with model teams before release forces you to make the framework more general. Every time we did this, the codebase got cleaner, because we had to separate what is truly model-specific from what belongs in the core scheduler, the memory manager, or the kernels.

And honestly, it's a two-way relationship. Model labs want their release to look good. If the inference stack is slow or broken on launch day, the benchmarks people post are the framework's numbers, not the model's true capability. So the labs have an incentive to collaborate early, share specs, sometimes even co-develop kernels. For an open-source project, that collaboration is one of the most valuable things you can have. It brings in expertise, it brings in contributors, and it means the first impression of the model, which often sticks, is a fast and correct one.

So I'd say Day-0 support is partly a product promise, partly a forcing function for good engineering, and partly a way of building the ecosystem relationships that keep an open-source project relevant.

r001.rationale: The response says users want to run new models immediately and may switch frameworks, but it does not clearly state that market demand determines Day-0 compatibility’s importance.

r002.rationale: The response mentions users, SGLang, and model labs collaborating, but it does not describe demand propagating from users through inference providers to Ying Sheng’s team and onward to model vendors.

astra-6.text:
Because the moment a new model is released, developers want to try it on their own workloads. If their infrastructure doesn’t support it yet, they have to wait or spend time building a workaround before they can even find out whether it’s useful.

Day-0 compatibility removes that delay. It lets people evaluate a new model immediately and make decisions based on what works for their application. It doesn’t mean every new model is automatically better, or that support on day one is fully optimized. It means the infrastructure is ready to let you experiment, while performance tuning can continue.

r001.rationale: The response says developers want to try new models immediately, but does not state that market demand determines Day-0 compatibility’s importance.

r002.rationale: It describes developers wanting access and infrastructure enabling experimentation, but omits the path from users through inference providers to Ying Sheng’s team and then model vendors.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the moment a new model comes out, developers want to try it on their own workloads. If their infrastructure doesn’t support it yet, they have to wait or spend time writing integration code before they can even find out whether it’s useful.

Day-0 compatibility removes that delay. It lets teams evaluate a new model immediately and make decisions based on quality, latency, and cost. It also gives them flexibility: as models improve, they can adopt the ones that work best for their applications without rebuilding their infrastructure each time.

r001.rationale: The response says developers want to try new models immediately, but does not state that market demand determines the importance of Day-0 compatibility.

r002.rationale: It describes developers seeking immediate access, but does not describe that demand propagating through inference providers to Ying Sheng’s team and then to model vendors.
